titre: A signal too regular to be natural
accroche: Jocelyn Bell spots in 1967 a pulsation of inexplicable regularity. They first named it “little green men”
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1967, Jocelyn Bell is a doctoral student at Cambridge. She has spent two years building, with her team, a radio telescope made of posts and cables spread over several hectares. The instrument spits out traces on paper, at the rate of thirty meters a day.

She goes through them by hand.

## A quarter of an inch on kilometers of paper

After a few weeks, she spots a trace that keeps coming back: a squiggle about a quarter of an inch long, always in the same region of the sky. It resembles neither the terrestrial interference she has learned to recognize, nor the scintillation she is supposed to be studying.

She asks for a faster recording to see the fine structure. The signal turns out to be a series of pulses separated by a little more than a second, of extraordinary regularity.

It is this regularity that poses the problem. Known astronomical objects vary, but not like a metronome. A clock in the sky points more toward a transmitter.

The team labels the source LGM, for *little green men*, with the humor of people who don’t believe it but cannot yet rule it out.

## How they ruled out the hypothesis

The elimination rests on a single observation, and it is decisive.

Bell methodically searches for other similar traces in her kilometers of paper. She finds a second source of the same type in another region of the sky. Then a third, a fourth. Two civilizations deciding to transmit at the same moment, on the same frequency, toward the same small English observatory, is a hypothesis that collapses on its own.

What remained was to explain what in nature can beat at that rate. The answer is a neutron star: the collapsed core of a massive star, a few kilometers across for the mass of the Sun, spinning on its axis and sweeping space with a beam. A lighthouse. Until then, these objects had been only a theoretical possibility.

## The prize

The 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics rewards the discovery of pulsars. It goes to Antony Hewish, Bell’s thesis advisor, and to Martin Ryle. Bell is not among them.

The omission was contested, and still is. Bell Burnell herself has always refused to make it a personal matter, judging that a prize rewards first and foremost the leadership of a program. She restated this position long after receiving, in 2018, another major honor, whose prize money she donated to doctoral scholarships.

One can grant her this view without endorsing the split. What the story shows is that the discovery came down to one precise act: someone refused to treat a quarter-inch anomaly as a nuisance.

repere.texte: Bell spots the first pulsation on November 28, 1967, going through by hand the paper traces of the radio telescope she helped build over two years. The 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics, which rewards this discovery, will go to Antony Hewish, her thesis advisor, and to Martin Ryle.
repere.source: University of Cambridge, “Journeys of discovery: Jocelyn Bell Burnell and pulsars,” 2019

carte.punch: A clock in the sky. They first called it “little green men.”
carte.idee: Jocelyn Bell spots in 1967 pulses with metronome regularity. What ruled out the hypothesis of an artificial signal: she found others elsewhere in the sky. They were rotating neutron stars.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Physics World — Overlooked for the Nobel: Jocelyn Bell Burnell
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: In English; traces the controversy and the subject’s own position.

quiz.question: What ruled out the hypothesis of an artificial signal?
choix: The discovery of other similar sources elsewhere in the sky
The signal’s irregularity, incompatible with a built transmitter
The immediate identification of a neutron star at that position
The signal’s disappearance as soon as the instrument was recalibrated
quiz.explication: Bell methodically searched for other similar traces in her kilometers of paper, and found some: several civilizations transmitting simultaneously toward the same observatory is not a tenable hypothesis. The signal was, on the contrary, perfectly regular, and the explanation by neutron stars came only afterward.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How long did Bell and her team take to build the radio telescope used for the discovery?
choix: Six months, reusing the antennas of an already existing observatory
Two years, with posts and cables spread over several hectares
Ten years, as part of a program funded by NASA
Only a few weeks, before data analysis began
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Bell spent two years, with her team, building a radio telescope made of posts and cables spread over several hectares, before even beginning to go through the traces it produced.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What, in the signal Bell spotted, immediately posed a problem?
choix: Its extreme faintness, barely detectable even with a fast recording
Its total resemblance to already known terrestrial interference
Its extraordinary regularity, like a metronome, whereas known astronomical objects vary otherwise
Its appearance in a region of the sky already mapped by another observatory
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Known astronomical objects vary, but not like a metronome; it is this extraordinary regularity, a clock in the sky, that points more toward a transmitter and immediately poses a problem.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is a neutron star, the explanation ultimately adopted for the signal?
choix: A cloud of interstellar gas that pulsates at regular intervals under the effect of gravity
A double star whose two components eclipse each other at regular intervals
A rotating black hole that emits a radio signal each time matter passes
The collapsed core of a massive star, a few kilometers across, that spins while sweeping space with a beam
quiz_supplementaire.explication: A neutron star is the collapsed core of a massive star, a few kilometers across for the mass of the Sun, spinning on its axis and sweeping space with a beam, like a lighthouse.
